page.layout: One page of running text in a single column, with no marginal notes. Top left: page number 150. Top centre: running head DIALECTICAE. Main text in one column, a chapter heading centred mid-page, then the woodcut-initialed paragraph. Bottom right: catchword "liquid".

main_text.p: causa est. Cæsar vicit Pompeium: Cæsar fuit victor Pompeij.

Quid igitur de iis quæ de futuro aliquid dicunt, deque eo quod possit fieri, aut non possit: de quibus Cicero in libro de Fato quæstionem logicæ artis obscurissimam esse scribit? Sanè disputari posset, non verè & proprie illas Enuntiationes esse. primùm quia non sunt habitus: deinde quia Medij, quod est quasi norma diiudicandæ conuenientiæ inter subiectũ & attributum, de quo in Argumentationibus intelliges: adhiberi ad ea quæ non sunt, non potest. Sed quoniam rerũ naturalium certus quidam ordo est à Deo constitutus, cuius propterea certus videtur euétus, vt in Solis & Lunæ defectionibus, quarum causæ naturales sunt: propterea fatius est, illas Philosophorum argutias non attingere,
main_text.head: Diuisio Enuntiationum. CAP. X.
main_text.p: VOTVPLEX[?] est Enuntiatio? Duplex. Vna quæ est simplex, quâ Græci ti[?] κατηγορικῶ[?] vocant: altera copulata, quâ iidem συνθετικῶ[?] appellant.
Quæ est Simplex? Quæ de uno tantùm, idque purè & absolutè vel affirmat, vel negat. vt Iuti, Mors est horribilis, mors non est horribilis, Filius heres esto. Filius exheres esto.
Quæ est prima diuisio simplicis Enuntia-tionis? Vt alia sit affirmatiua, quæ vnum a-

page.notes: Long s (s) normalised to plain s throughout, so "caussa" appears as "causa" and "est" as "est". Printed "caussa" with double s may be a 16th/17th-century spelling; the form on the scan is uncertain. Woodcut initial at the start of the Enuntiatio paragraph: first letter uncertain, transcribed as V[?]. Greek in the Græci sentence is only partly legible: "ti" at the start of the line after "Græ-" is uncertain, and the Greek words κατηγορικῶ and συνθετικῶ are my best reading and are marked [?]. "Iuti" is printed as shown; the reading is uncertain. The catchword "liquid" is the last line on the page, set at the right, and is not repeated in the text.
